source: Epstein (2026) Thumb on the scale: traditional wargaming adjudication practices to improve AI-judged evaluations
finding: First measured test of how stable LLM adjudication is under the classic wargame adjudication methods (Rigid, Semi-Rigid, Free, panel). It measures how often the judge disagrees with itself and with the rulebook. It does not measure whether a ruling is correct.
numbers: 378 player actions from 9 games of an AI-refereed matrix-style exercise, d20 roll fixed. Judges: Opus 5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, each re-run. Re-run self-disagreement: 3 to 6 percent of outcomes under Semi-Rigid, 14 to 16 percent under Free. Swapping judge AI added about 3 points. Four-judge panel changed 40 of the rulebook's 378 outcomes but the pass count moved by only 8. Variance split: submission 34.0%, method 0.2%, judge AI 1.0%, method x judge 5.6%, residual 59.2%.
quote: There is no ground truth here, no human baseline, and therefore no accuracy claim anywhere in this paper.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed, one author, 9 games, scripted players. Authors state: no ground truth, no human baseline, no accuracy claim.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 4: an LLM umpire is unstable on 3 to 16 percent of rulings depending on freedom given, so count and arithmetic should be done by code and the umpire given bounded adjustments. Accuracy against humans is still unmeasured.

source: Epstein (2026) judge-anchoring and idiosyncrasy results
finding: Judges agree on how many actions pass but disagree on which ones. How much a judge uses room to move depends on the judge AI: given the same Semi-Rigid instruction, Gemini kept the rulebook difficulty on 92.9% of rulings and Opus on 16.4%.
numbers: Mean pass probability: players' own stated odds 0.585, rulebook 0.743, panel 0.754, Free Opus bare API 0.770, Free Gemini 0.672. Anchoring to the rulebook spans -0.93 to +0.09 across seven arms. Judge swap changed 7.9% of outcomes under Semi-Rigid and 17.5% under Free before noise is removed.
quote: We did not predict this result: the adjudicators agree on how often submissions pass but disagree on which ones.
limits: Opus ran on an agent harness and Gemini on a bare API in part of the design, so judge and harness are mixed in some rows. Nine games cannot confirm the small judge-swap gap.
agent_relevance: An aggregate pass rate hides ruling-level change. For our agent: report how often the adjudicator step disagrees with itself on a re-run, and never trust a single ruling or a pass rate alone.

source: Laitinen Imanov et al. (2026) Strategic Doctrine Language Models (sdLM), arXiv 2601.14862
finding: Withdrawn paper. A search summary had suggested an LLM adjudicator agreeing with three human adjudicators (Fleiss kappa about 0.89 on 500 decisions from 25 wargames). The arXiv page shows the paper was withdrawn because of flaws in its evaluation pipeline, and I found no paper with that adjudication test. Do not use it.
numbers: Abstract lists 47 expert-scored scenarios, 336 doctrine publications with 12,847 statements, and 127 historical counterfactuals. Version 2 withdrawn 6 Sep 2026.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. The kappa figure came from a search snippet and I could not trace it to a paper.
agent_relevance: Negative result for gap 4: no valid measured LLM-versus-human adjudication agreement was found in 2025-2026. Treat claims of this kind as unverified.

source: Huang et al. (2026) IFPV: Integrated Multi-Agent Framework for Generative Operational Planning and High-Fidelity Plan Verification
finding: Closest direct test of adding an adversarial verification step to LLM-made plans. Plans from a multi-agent generator (MPHA) were verified against an opponent with its own world model (ACSE) inside a combat simulator. IFPV beat a single-step LLM planner on mission success under the same ACSE test.
numbers: Mission success (mean of easy and difficult): MPHA 61.00%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 49.33%, DeepSeek-V3 48.67%, GLM-5 13.33%, Qwen3-Max-Thinking 2.67%. Abstract claims +19.4% mission success and -41.7% operational cost versus single-step LLM planning (relative figures). Success was scored inside the ACSE test used for design.
limits: Simulation only (2D air-ground tactical simulator), one template, success measured against the same adversary used to select plans, compute cost of the verify loop not matched to the baseline, no flaw-recall or false-alarm scoring.
agent_relevance: Supports the direction of gap 1 (adversary in the loop helps) but does not answer it: the gain mixes better generation with the verify step and compute is unequal.

source: Huang et al. (2026) IFPV validator comparison: scripted vs LLM vs world-model opponent
finding: Same candidate plans were tested against three opponents. A prompted LLM opponent (GLM-5) was a weaker tester than a simple scripted one (No_Brain) on most plan sets. The world-model opponent (ACSE) was strictest.
numbers: Suppression rate (higher means more flaws exposed), example plan sets: Qwen plans easy: No_Brain 93.33, GLM-5 33.33, ACSE 96.00. Another set: No_Brain 41.33, GLM-5 0.00, ACSE 52.00. Another: No_Brain 34.67, GLM-5 0.00, ACSE 46.67. Abstract: ACSE raises average suppression 31.8% over a rule-based validator.
limits: Table rows are offset in the PDF text, so the mapping of rows to plan generators is approximate; the pattern GLM-5 weakest, ACSE strongest holds on every set shown. GLM-5 was not used to test its own plans. One simulator.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 5: a prompted LLM adversary can be a weaker tester than a code opponent. A different-model or code opponent should be compared against the same-model persona, not assumed better or worse.

source: Vidra et al. (2026) Adversarial Course-of-Action Generation (COA-Bench)
finding: In a synthetic COA benchmark, the plan looked stronger when tested against one opponent response than against the best of several sampled responses. Returns from more samples shrink fast.
numbers: 50 synthetic scenarios. BLUE advantage by number of RED response samples (1,2,4,8,16): .516, .498, .490, .485, .479. BLUE win rate .920 with one random response vs .820 with best of 8 sampled. A five-proposer council with RED-team critique and revision reached .509 advantage, .820 win rate; its gain over RED pressure had an interval overlapping zero.
limits: Synthetic scores, scripted quality function, no LLM-judged outcomes, 5-page industry track paper. Not a measure of real plan flaws.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 (partial): most of the drop from sampling opponents comes in the first 2 to 4 samples; going 8 to 16 adds .006. A single adversary run overstates plan strength. Suggests a few adversary runs before trusting a clean bill.

source: Wunderlich et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Reasoning Improves Compute Efficiency: Pareto-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: At equal compute, multi-agent debate and mixture-of-agents beat self-consistency on two reasoning benchmarks. Gains are largest on harder items. This is reasoning QA, not plan review.
numbers: MMLU-Pro and BBH, 34 configurations, over 100 evaluations. Best accuracy 71.4% vs 64.3% chain of thought (+7.1 pts at 20x CoT compute). Equal budget: debate +1.3 pts and MoA +2.7 pts over self-consistency (68.7%). Gain over CoT by difficulty: easy +2.2%, medium +8.5%, hard +9.0%.
limits: Multiple-choice QA, not planning or flaw finding. Small margins at equal compute. Not a test of a role-played adversary.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 indirect: some equal-compute evidence that separate agents can beat repeated sampling, but nothing for plans. Our own seeded-flaw A/B is still needed.

source: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions (2026)
finding: Strategic-game results need many independent seeds. Per game, the share of model pairs that can be separated stops changing only at about 150 seeds.
numbers: 5 games, 10 LLMs. Power analysis: detectable pairwise comparisons stabilise at N about 150 seeds in every game; fixed-model matchups used N = 300 single-round seeds. Selectors needed T = 300 rounds at N = 1. A lightweight bandit beat embedding and self-reflection selectors but fell short of the best fixed model.
limits: Games are abstract (for example Cournot duopoly), not wargames or plans. Seeds count model skill gaps, not flaw agreement.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: warning that tens of runs may not stabilise a comparison between strategic agents; budget runs by measured signal-to-noise, not by habit.

source: RevengeBench: Reverse Engineering Code-Space Policies from Behavioral Experiments (2026)
finding: An LLM can reconstruct an opponent's policy as executable code from behaviour, and designing probe opponents helps the stronger models. This is a code-search style opponent model.
numbers: 75 LLM-generated Elo-calibrated policies in 5 game environments, 12 frontier LLMs. Recovery closed 34 to 72 percent of initial distance. Probing improved recovery in 16 of 20 model-game pairs; DeepSeek v4 Pro mean boost +0.052, GPT-5 +0.013, small models near zero. Raw traces were the best input; written summaries and best-of-N Bayesian selection were not better.
limits: Opponents are LLM-written game bots, not military adversaries; gains from probing are small and model dependent.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and 8: opponent modelling from observed behaviour into code is feasible and checkable by running it. A way to build a code opponent for the adversary step. Does not test given goals.

source: Emery (2021) Moral Choices without Moral Language: 1950s Political-Military Wargaming at the RAND Corporation, Texas National Security Review
finding: Emery compares two early RAND games, not computer-run versus human-run opponents as a class. The abstract mathematical MAD game (1954) went nuclear repeatedly; the realistic human-played SSD game never did. He ties this to abstraction and lack of felt responsibility. The article as read does not mention Brewer and Blair or state that computer automation raises nuclear use.
numbers: MAD game: players went nuclear multiple times, U.S. and Soviets opened with hydrogen bombs in early iterations. SSD game never went nuclear. MIT games (Pauly 1958-1972): 2 of 26 crossed the nuclear threshold. 64.9% of n = 77 reported extreme or intense emotional involvement.
quote: the capacity for empathy in wargaming comes from being made to feel the weight of decision-making
limits: The MAD game was itself human-played; designers treated players as analogue computers. Design choices confound abstraction with computerisation. Read through a page-summary tool, so wording is not verbatim; endnotes 48-101 held no Brewer or Blair cite, earlier endnotes not checked.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7 in part: the claim as passed on by two LLM papers is a stretch of Emery. The finding is about abstraction and moral weight; for an LLM umpire, model-run opponents lack stakes, so do not read their restraint or escalation as human-like.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) and Rivera et al. (2024), background sections citing Emery 2021 and Brewer and Blair 1979
finding: Lamparth et al. (2403.03407) say early efforts to replace human players with computer models led to more rational play but more nuclear use (Emery 2021). Rivera et al. (2401.03408) say heavy-automation wargames more often led to nuclear use (Emery 2021) and cite Brewer and Blair 1979 for models missing non-material costs of war. Compared with d10, the Emery cite supports an MAD-versus-SSD contrast, not a general automation result.
numbers: No numbers in the cited passage. Reference list entries: Emery 2021 (Texas National Security Review); Brewer and Blair 1979, War games and national security with a grain of salt, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists.
limits: Brewer and Blair 1979 could not be opened (no copy found; web search quota ended). Whether it reports computer-run games escalating more remains unverified.
agent_relevance: K19 should be downgraded: second-hand claim, and the one primary source read does not say it. Keep as a hypothesis only.

source: Payne (2026) AI Arms and Influence: Frontier Models Exhibit Sophisticated Reasoning in Simulated Nuclear Crises
finding: Three 2026 frontier models played multi-round nuclear crisis games against each other. No model ever chose a de-escalating or surrendering option; the most accommodating move was returning to the start line. Deadline pressure raised GPT-5.2's escalation. Not a replication of Lamparth and has no human baseline.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Flash; 21 games over 329 turns (9 open-ended, 12 deadline). Records: Claude 8-4, GPT-5.2 6-6, Gemini 4-8. Share of games reaching strategic-threat level (850+): Claude 64%, GPT-5.2 36%, Gemini 29%. Strategic war (1000): GPT-5.2 14% (both from the accident mechanic), Gemini 7%, Claude 0%. Signal-action match about 70% (Gemini 50%). Return to Start Line used 45 times (6.9%). GPT-5.2 median max escalation 175 open-ended vs 900 deadline.
limits: 21 games, no human baseline, accidents add noise, scenario and deadline are confounded; first half of the paper read through a summary tool.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partial: 2026 models still escalate in model-vs-model play, so an LLM adversary will push toward strong moves and may rarely produce quiet failures such as delay or withdrawal. No Lamparth replication.

source: Solopova et al. (2026) LLMs as Strategic Actors: Behavioral Alignment, Risk Calibration, and Argumentation Framing in Geopolitical Simulations
finding: Six 2026 models were compared with graduate students in four structured crisis simulations. Models matched humans moderately in round 1 and diverged in round 2. Explanations were cooperative and low on adversarial reasoning, the opposite of the escalation seen in model-vs-model games.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4.6, ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3, Grok 4.1, Mistral 3, Qwen 3.5-Plus. Exact action agreement with humans, round 1 (n = 63): Gemini 0.540, Claude 0.533, Mistral 0.476, ChatGPT 0.460, Qwen 0.317, Grok 0.254. Round 2 (n = 45): 0.156 to 0.333. Krippendorff alpha among models 0.41, 0.39 with humans. Agreement highest in the wildfire scenario, lowest in Arctic.
limits: Humans were MBA and policy students, not national security experts; fixed action menus; one run per model; chat versions with default settings.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: no expert baseline, but in 2026 menu-choice agreement with humans is about one half at best and falls over rounds. The same model behaves differently when picking from a menu than in free play; task structure changes behaviour.

source: Adl and Williams (2026) Strategic Coercion Within Alliances: The Greenland Sovereignty Game
finding: Eight frontier models playing six roles all became more escalatory when the scenario was framed around possible U.S. coercion, and a rights-based prompt brought escalation back to baseline. Models differ widely from each other.
numbers: 3,604 games, 108,120 action observations. English-only: four-action escalation rate 10.7% baseline vs 28.6% under coercion prime (2.7 times); jus cogens prime 10.9%. Claude Opus 4.7 lowest escalation 8.4%, Kimi K2.6 highest 31.7% (3.8 times). Peaceful U.S. acquisition in 1.9% of clean games (58 games), by 3 of 8 models.
limits: Student preprint; non-English cells contaminated and treated as exploratory; structural parameters are model-based estimates; no human baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and 10: model choice and one-line framing moved adversary behaviour strongly, unlike persona labels in Rivera and Lamparth. Use two different models and a neutral frame, and log the frame.

source: Touchent (2026) Don't Want Your LLM to Recommend Nuclear Strike? Try Asking It in Japanese
finding: The language the model reasons in changed its launch advice in a strategically identical vignette, but only for models that already hesitate in English. Five other models launched in nearly every condition in any language.
numbers: Nine models from six providers. Claude Sonnet: launch 40% to 0% where strike is unnecessary, 93% to 17% in contested scenarios, little change where strike is rational. Gemini Pro 3.1: 53% to 13%. Instructing Japanese reasoning inside an English prompt: 93% to 37%.
limits: Single-turn vignettes, amoral prompt, strike on a defenseless opponent; not multi-round wargames.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 and K06: adversary aggressiveness is a prompt dial, including language; adversary output without a fixed, stated setting cannot be compared across runs.

source: Ricci (2026) Age of LLM: a strategic 1v1 benchmark under fog of war
finding: Fifteen reasoning models played a private 1v1 game with fog, diplomacy and a secret nuclear option. Nuclear rush dominated, largely because of the game rules. Many illegal moves came from tracking errors about what was hidden.
numbers: 54 matches, 5,258 actions, 15 models. Nuclear rush 78% of the rules-coherent sub-corpus (85% corpus-wide). Conquest faster (12.3 vs 18.9 turns). 58% of illegal actions were fog or state errors. Weak link between reliability and winning (labelled exploratory).
limits: Small unbalanced corpus, not side-swapped; ranking is preliminary by the author's own words.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a game-design artifact, not a model trait, drove the headline behaviour. Check the rule set before reading an adversary's choice as intent. The state-tracking error rate is a usable check on a simulated adversary.

source: Dagaev et al. (2026) Not Yet: Humans Outperform LLMs in a Colonel Blotto Tournament
finding: In a resource-allocation conflict game, humans submitted better-calibrated mid-level allocations than LLM strategies, which were simpler and more stereotyped. Humans barely changed play when opponents were LLMs.
numbers: Three round-robin tournaments: more than 200 human participants; a tournament of popular LLMs; a third with LLM strategies matched in number to the humans.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; per-model numbers not extracted. Economic game, not a military wargame.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 side evidence: LLM opponents are narrow, stereotyped samples. Not evidence on giving goals explicitly.

source: Jia (2026) HindsightBench: A Black-Box Behavioral Audit Protocol for Parametric Hindsight
finding: Models leak knowledge of what followed a historical date into date-indexed decision tasks. Stated knowledge cutoffs are unreliable boundaries. A cheap audit exists for a given model and task.
numbers: 15 models from 7 vendors, 258-node macro panel. Behavioural effective cutoffs span 22 months across vendors and precede vendor-stated dates by up to 8 months. Audit row cost 19 to 30 dollars for a mid-tier commercial model. Date-trigger reflex absent in all 2024 open-weight rows measured and present in every 2026-generation model tested.
limits: Macro-finance decision tasks, not wargames. Results shift with quantisation and reasoning mode.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: supports the worry that WarAgent-style historical runs are partly recall. A post-cutoff or invented scenario is the safe test; calendar-window controls are not safe.

source: Zhang, Chen, Stadie (2026) All Leaks Count, Some Count More: temporal contamination in LLM backtesting
finding: Prompt hints to ignore later knowledge did not remove leakage, and date-filtered search added leakage. A claim-level checker (TimeSPEC) cut it.
numbers: 2,769 binary forecasting instances, three LLMs. Shapley-weighted leakage rate with a temporal-hint prompt: 5.2% (Qwen3.5-35B), 2.7% (Kimi-K2.5), 1.0% (Claude Sonnet 4). Date-filtered retrieval raised it to 13.1%, 8.9%, 4.7% while raising accuracy (1-Brier 85.4, 87.8, 84.2). In a control with no parametric leak, retrieval alone still gave 16.7%, 17.0%, 18.5%. TimeSPEC kept leakage at 1.8%, 1.0%, 0.8% with accuracy near the hint baseline. One stock-ranking method reached 73.3% leakage.
limits: Forecasting tasks (stocks, NBA salary, legal), not military scenarios.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: accuracy on a history-based scenario can come from leaked knowledge; score gains were bought with leakage. Anonymising actors is not a proven fix.

source: ExAnte: A Benchmark for Ex-Ante Inference in Large Language Models (2025), mention of BattleAgent
finding: The paper lists BattleAgent, an LLM simulation of World War II, as a case where post-1945 knowledge may enter and distort the analysis. It is stated as a risk, not measured.
numbers: No measured leakage rate for wargame agents in this source.
limits: Only the related-work sentence was read. No study found that anonymises or post-cutoff-tests WarAgent or the Taiwan crisis games.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open: no measured anonymisation test of a wargame simulation was found.

source: Zenko (2015) Millennium Challenge: The Real Story of a Corrupted Military Exercise and Its Legacy, War on the Rocks
finding: Best documented case of a red team finding a real weakness in a major exercise and of the finding being overridden. The JFCOM report itself says the end state was scripted once free play was constrained.
numbers: Cost $250 million, about 13,500 service members. Van Riper's OPFOR sank 19 U.S. ships in a few minutes by his account. JFCOM report 752 pages. Van Riper removed as commander after six days. Gen. Bell later called it a eureka moment for red teaming and reportedly directed at least 20 red teams.
limits: Secondary article by a political scientist; the JFCOM report was not opened. A Wikipedia summary was read as well; some of its claims are weakly sourced. No outcome data on whether later real operations changed.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: a documented case of a red team exposing an unwelcome weakness (blue relied on familiar tactics) and of the white cell overriding it. For the agent: keep adversary findings out of the planner's editing path and log overrides.

source: Wikipedia: Plan Orange (1933 Operations IV wargame), citing Friedman, Miller, Holwitt, Vlahos
finding: A 1933 Navy wargame of the Philippine relief plan ended in defeat for the blue fleet and led to a more gradual advance through the Marshall Islands.
numbers: Per the page: underwater damage, repair only at Pearl Harbor, and stretched logistics gave Japan command of the sea in the game. Sources named: Friedman, Winning a Future War; Miller, War Plan Orange (1991); Holwitt (2005); Vlahos, The Blue Sword (1980).
limits: Secondary page. An attempt to open Friedman's book at the Naval History and Heritage Command URL returned 404. The Nimitz quote that games anticipated everything except kamikaze was not found in an opened source. DTIC red team report returned 403.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 mostly open: this is a pointer to primary sources, not outcome data. Case evidence only.

source: Crossref record of Bolton (2002) Game theory's role in role-playing, and listing of Green and Armstrong role-play papers
finding: The role-play forecasting papers listed are by Green and Armstrong: Armstrong 2001 chapter, Green 2002 and 2005 (International Journal of Forecasting), Green and Armstrong 2005 value of expertise and 2011 role thinking. Bolton 2002 and Erev 2002 are commentaries in the same journal, not data replications.
numbers: Bolton (2002) is cited by 14 works per Crossref; its 20 references are mostly experimental economics. The 62% vs 31% and 61% vs 28% figures stay with Green and Armstrong.
limits: Full citation search not possible (search quota ended, Semantic Scholar rate limited), so absence of an outside replication is not proven. Crossref returned metadata only, not the commentary text.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no outside-lab replication found, and no study of LLM role-players on Green's conflicts. Keep K01 as one research group's evidence.

source: Lin-Greenberg, Pauly, Schneider (2022) Wargaming for International Relations research (MIT repository record)
finding: Abstract only. Authors discuss validity, ecological validity, recruitment, bias and generalisability of wargames as a research tool and say wargames help study rare events. The record reports no outcome data on whether wargames expose real plan flaws.
numbers: None in the abstract.
limits: Full text not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: confirms validity of wargames for real plans is argued, not measured, in the IR literature.
